issues.legal_issue: A delegated rule-making authority cannot give a rule retrospective effect unless the enabling law expressly or by necessary implication authorizes retrospective rule-making.
material_facts: The governing rule provided for compensation of a displaced person with a verified agricultural-land claim, as far as possible, by allotment of agricultural land.
An amendment added an explanation limiting agricultural land under the rules to land in a rural area and purported to deem the explanation always to have been inserted.
The government relied on the retrospective explanation to cancel an allotment of land that was in an urban area.
The enabling Act authorized rules to carry out its purposes but contained no express or implied authority to make rules with retrospective effect.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective operation of the explanation was beyond the rule-making power; it could operate only prospectively from the date it was added. The cancellation orders based on it were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of delegated rule-making power is governed by the enabling provision, and subordinate legislation cannot operate retrospectively without express authorization or authorization by necessary implication. The Court relied on section 40 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and referred to Cannapore Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. v. Collector of Customs and Central Excise, Cochin, The Income Tax Officer, Alleppy v. M. C. Ponnoose, and B. S. Vadera v. Union of India, distinguishing the latter because the language of article 309 supported retrospective rules in that case.

rule.if: delegated_rule_challenge and enabling_law_lacks_retroactive_authority and rule_given_retroactive_effect and decision_relies_on_retroactive_rule

predicates.delegated_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule made by an authority exercising delegated rule-making power.
predicates.enabling_law_lacks_retroactive_authority: The law granting rule-making power does not authorize retrospective rules expressly or by necessary implication.
predicates.rule_given_retroactive_effect: The rule purports to apply to a period before it was made or amended.
predicates.decision_relies_on_retroactive_rule: The challenged decision relies on the rule's purported retrospective operation.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns delegated rules, the enabling law provides no authority for retrospective rule-making, and a decision relies on a rule's retrospective operation, that retrospective effect is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: Parliamentary laying of a delegated rule does not prevent a court from reviewing whether the rule exceeds the authority granted by the enabling law.
material_facts: The enabling Act required rules to be laid before each House of Parliament and allowed the Houses to modify or annul them.
The government relied on the laying requirement in support of the validity of the retrospectively operating amendment.
The Court held that laying the rules did not prevent judicial scrutiny of whether they conformed to the enabling Act.
issues.conclusion: Laying a rule before Parliament does not bar courts from scrutinizing its validity or holding it ultra vires if it exceeds the rule-making power.
issues.legal_principle: A parliamentary laying procedure under which a rule remains effective unless modified or annulled does not validate a rule that exceeds the authority delegated by the enabling Act, nor does it oust judicial review. The Court referred to section 40(3) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and to Craies on Statute Law, Sixth Edition, pages 304–306, on forms of laying.

predicates.delegated_rule_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a rule made under delegated authority.
predicates.rule_subject_to_parliamentary_laying: The rule is required to be laid before a legislature under a procedure allowing legislative modification or annulment.
predicates.rule_alleged_beyond_delegated_authority: The challenge asserts that the rule exceeds the authority granted by the enabling law.

issues.definition: When a delegated rule is subject to parliamentary laying and is challenged as exceeding delegated authority, courts may review its validity.
